tests.name: Effective description
tests.reasoning: The description starts with 'Use this skill when the user wants to understand or cut Amazon Bedrock spend, or check Bedrock capacity, even if they don't call it a cost review' which is imperative phrasing and focuses on user intent. It explicitly lists many trigger contexts (high/low bills, token drift, PT idle/oversized, quota headroom, throttling, invocation-log retention, pasted CloudWatch/Cost Explorer output) covering cases where the user doesn't name the domain directly, and ends with a scope exclusion ('Not for outages happening now'). While long, it remains a single flowing sentence/short paragraph structure typical of dense trigger-rich skill descriptions, and every clause serves to map user phrasing to the skill's applicability rather than describing internal implementation.
tests.evidence: "Use this skill when the user wants to understand or cut Amazon Bedrock spend, or check Bedrock capacity, even if they don't call it a cost review, for example why the bill is high or suspiciously low..."

tests.name: Verbosity and conciseness
tests.reasoning: The body is dense with domain-specific rules, API quirks, and exact field names rather than explaining general concepts. It assumes AWS/Bedrock knowledge and jumps straight into project-specific conventions like usage-type matching, token labeling, and quota naming.
tests.evidence: Group, don't filter: product-attribute filters and `--dimension-key` are rejected.

tests.name: Detailed reference materials must not be in body
tests.reasoning: While the body contains many specific facts, these are short, non-exhaustive guidance rules and pointers to detailed reference files rather than large embedded reference tables; the bulk of detail (quota codes, full check tables, cloudwatch alarm specs) is pushed to references/.

tests.name: Reference files must be linked
tests.reasoning: Every file in references/ is linked via markdown links in the body.

tests.name: Reference links must specify when to load
tests.reasoning: Each reference link is tied to a specific trigger condition (step number, check type, or scenario) rather than a generic 'see for details' mention.
tests.evidence: [cost-analysis.md](references/cost-analysis.md) (Steps 3–5, before any LLM-COST or LLM-PT finding); [checks-model-invocation.md](references/checks-model-invocation.md) (before LLM-INV-002/007)

tests.name: Reference path format
tests.reasoning: All reference links use relative paths rooted at references/ with no absolute paths or traversal.

tests.name: Prescription vs description
tests.reasoning: Fragile operations (billed vs estimated labeling, quota code lookup, token reconciliation) are given exact prescriptive rules, while flexible analysis portions (e.g., deciding LLM-COST-003/004) are framed with reasoning ('decide ... from the invocation pattern and the stated workload') rather than rigid steps.
tests.evidence: decide 003/004 from the invocation pattern and the stated workload, at catalog severity.

tests.name: Defaults, not menus
tests.reasoning: The Router table and procedure consistently specify a 'First read' default for each scenario rather than listing multiple equal options, and rate lookup order is explicitly prioritized.
tests.evidence: Rates, in order: the user (say so); `pricing:GetProducts` ... or the [pricing page](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/) read with `verify_aws_claim`.

tests.name: Favor procedures over declarations
tests.reasoning: The procedure teaches a generalizable method (scope, tokens, cost model, coverage check, checks, PT, headroom, alarms) applicable to any Bedrock cost review, not a one-off instance-specific task.
tests.evidence: Run the steps in order. Each step is bounded: a denied API, no datapoints or an unsupported region is recorded as `unavailable` / `not checked` and the review goes on.
